name: Phantom Bandwidth
description:
Phantom Bandwidth is built around the aesthetic of lost, degraded, and discontinued transmission infrastructure—the musical equivalent of archaeology conducted through broken radios. Artists compose by layering functional music over simulated or genuine recordings of dead carrier signals, obsolete codec artifacts, and the specific degradation patterns of communication technologies that GLMZ has discarded as it expanded. The genre treasures imperfection as artifact: a piece might be intentionally transmitted through outdated relay hardware specifically to acquire the distortion signature of that equipment before being released. The gap between what the music was and what the transmission has made it becomes the composition.

A defining characteristic of Phantom Bandwidth is its use of 'ghost data'—the faint, sometimes decipherable remains of previous transmissions that physically occupy the same frequency infrastructure as the new work. Skilled Phantom Bandwidth composers treat these recovered fragments—a word from a decades-old personal message, a chord from a long-deleted broadcast—as collaborators, building compositions around whatever the infrastructure has retained. This practice has occasionally produced legally complicated situations when recovered fragments are identified as belonging to individuals who did not consent to inclusion, though the genre community largely treats such discoveries as ethically neutral acts of salvage.
creator: various
tier_availability: All tiers; most authentic work originates in infrastructure-rich Tiers 4-6 where old relay hardware is accessible
legality: Generally legal; ghost data recovery exists in a contested regulatory gray zone under data residency statutes
audience: Infrastructure workers, communications historians, electronic music experimentalists, urban archaeologists, nostalgia communities
cultural_impact: Phantom Bandwidth has unexpectedly become the genre most associated with the emotional experience of urban obsolescence in GLMZ—the feeling that the city's continuous forward motion erases not just buildings and systems but the lives that ran through them. Its influence has crossed into architecture and urban design discourse, with some city planners citing Phantom Bandwidth aesthetics when arguing for the preservation of legacy infrastructure. Several pieces in the genre are now treated as unintentional historical records after the ghost data they incorporated proved to be the only surviving documentation of events that official archives lack.
story_hooks: A Phantom Bandwidth artist recovers a ghost data fragment from a decommissioned relay that appears to be an encrypted distress call from someone who officially never existed
A corporation quietly purchases the rights to a specific frequency range used by a beloved Phantom Bandwidth artist, forcing them off the infrastructure that defines their sound
Two artists simultaneously release pieces built around the same ghost data fragment, leading to a dispute about who discovered it first and what ethical obligations accompany that claim
